groups.directions:
Topic: Sentence Improvement
Subtopic: Grammar Improvement

questions.text: He is not only an excellent researcher, **but also he teaches well**.
questions.explanation: The correlative conjunction "not only... but also" must link parallel grammatical structures. Since "not only" is followed by a noun phrase ("an excellent researcher"), "but also" must also be followed by a noun phrase ("a good teacher").

questions.text: If you had listened to my advice, you **would not be in** this terrible situation right now.
questions.explanation: This is a mixed conditional sentence. The "if" clause is in the past perfect (referring to a past action), and the main clause uses "would + base verb" (referring to a present result: "right now"). The sentence is grammatically correct as is.

questions.text: The board of directors **have unanimously approved** the merger with the rival company.
questions.explanation: The phrase "board of directors" refers to a single collective entity acting together (indicated by "unanimously"). Therefore, it takes a singular verb "has".

questions.text: Hardly had the play started **than the power went** out in the entire theater.
questions.explanation: The conjunction "Hardly" is always paired with "when", not "than". "Than" is used with "No sooner".

questions.text: None of the applicants **were able to pass** the rigorous physical examination.
questions.explanation: In formal written English and strict grammar rules for competitive exams, "None of" followed by a plural noun should preferably take a singular verb ("was") to emphasize "not a single one". (Though "were" is acceptable in informal usage, "was" is the strictly correct grammatical improvement).

groups.directions:
Topic: Sentence Improvement
Subtopic: Grammar Improvement

questions.text: Between you and **I, I believe** that the project is doomed to fail.
questions.explanation: "Between" is a preposition, and pronouns following a preposition must be in the objective case ("me"). The subject of the next clause remains "I". So, "Between you and me, I believe".

questions.text: She is one of the few women who **has successfully climbed** Mount Everest without supplemental oxygen.
questions.explanation: In the phrase "one of the [plural noun] who", the relative pronoun "who" refers to the plural noun ("women"). Therefore, the verb following "who" must be plural ("have").

questions.text: It is high time you **start preparing** for your upcoming final examinations.
questions.explanation: The phrase "It is high time" is always followed by a clause in the simple past tense to indicate something that is already overdue. "Start" must be improved to "started".

questions.text: He asked me what **was the time** and where the nearest train station was.
questions.explanation: In an indirect question, the word order must be assertive (Subject + Verb), not interrogative (Verb + Subject). "What was the time" should be improved to "what the time was".

questions.text: I am not used **to wake up** so early in the morning on weekends.
questions.explanation: When "used to" is preceded by a "be" verb (am/is/are/was/were) meaning "accustomed to", it functions as a preposition and must be followed by a gerund (-ing form). "To wake" becomes "to waking".

groups.directions:
Topic: Sentence Improvement
Subtopic: Grammar Improvement

questions.text: The teacher, along with all her students, **are going on** a field trip to the museum tomorrow.
questions.explanation: When two subjects are connected by phrases like "along with," "as well as," or "in addition to," the verb must agree with the primary (first) subject. "The teacher" is singular, so the verb must be "is".

questions.text: Having finished his homework, **the TV was turned on** by John to watch his favorite show.

options.label: B
options.text: the TV had been turned on

options.label: C
options.text: turning on the TV was done

questions.explanation: This is a dangling modifier error. The participle phrase "Having finished his homework" must modify the subject of the main clause. The TV cannot finish homework; John did. The sentence must be rewritten in the active voice so "John" is the subject.

questions.text: I would rather stay indoors and read a book **than going out** in this freezing weather.
questions.explanation: The phrase "would rather" uses the base form of a verb ("stay"). To maintain parallelism, the verb following "than" must also be in the base form. "Going" must be improved to "go".

questions.text: By next December, my parents **will be married** for exactly thirty years.
questions.explanation: To describe an action or state that will have continued up to a specific point in the future ("By next December"), the future perfect tense must be used. "Will have been married" is the correct improvement.
